records.our_prose: Marigold inverts the usual companion framing: it is the plant you place to benefit others. Its one research-supported pest function is nematode suppression, and only in a specific form: French marigolds (Tagetes patula) grown as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months in the target bed and then incorporated, ahead of a susceptible crop, can reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations via root-released alpha-terthienyl. UF/IFAS is explicit that simply interplanting a few marigolds among vegetables has not been shown to reduce nematodes, and the African types are less effective than French for this. The broader reputation, that marigold scent repels insects, rabbits, and deer, is traditional companion lore: sometimes borne out, not reliably documented. What is solid is that marigold is a strong pollinator and beneficial-insect draw, so it earns its place as an insectary edge or border. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site for sun and airflow.

records.source_context: While it’s true that many marigolds produce the chemical alpha-terthienyl , shown to reduce certain populations of plant-parasitic nematodes, simply planting them alongside another crop (intercropping) has not been shown to reduce nematode populations. You can learn more about this topic in our article, “Garden Myths, Volume One.” Nonetheless, the marigold is a reliable Florida annual.

records.our_prose: In California's interior valleys, marigold is a long-season warm-weather bedding and edging plant: sow or transplant after the last frost into warm soil, and it blooms through the hot, dry summer to the first fall frost. Heat and sun are ideal, not stressful. Water deeply but let the soil dry between waterings, since the dry-summer climate suits marigold's drought tolerance and overwatering rots roots. Sow successively for a steady supply, and use a French marigold cover stand where root-knot nematodes are a problem.

records.source_context: Marigold can be grown ahead of time as a cover crop to suppress nematodes before planting a susceptible crop such as a vegetable crop. It also is a good choice to plant in ornamental planting beds where root-knot nematodes are a problem on other annuals. In order to be an effective cover crop in nematode management, marigold should be planted at least two months before the desired vegetable crop.

records.our_prose: In Hawaii and other frost-free tropical areas, marigolds bloom all year, loving the warmth and sun; just replace tired plants now and then. The humidity can bring gray mold on the big double flowers, so give them room for air and water at the soil. Marigolds are also grown in Hawaii as a cover crop to fight root-knot nematodes in the soil.

records.source_context: When planted as a cover crop, several marigold cultivars have been found to suppress root-knot nematodes in the soil. Best Marigold Cultivars for Nematode Suppression French marigold cultivars ‘Tangerine’ and ‘Single Gold’ ( Tagetes patula ‘Tangerine’, and Tagetes patula ‘Single Gold’) have shown resistance to several root-knot nematode species.

records.our_prose: Rotating marigolds is not as important as it is for vegetables, but it still helps. Plant them in a different spot each year if you can, and clean up old, diseased leaves at the end of the season. Used on purpose, a thick patch of French marigolds grown for a couple of months and then dug in is a real way to cut down soil nematodes before you plant vegetables there.

records.our_prose: Marigolds direct-sow readily into warm soil (about 65 to 70 °F) at 1/4 in depth and germinate in 5 to 8 days, the simplest method in long-season areas. To gain weeks or for the slow-developing tall African types, start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost (up to 8 weeks for African) and transplant after frost. Pinch tall African types once to encourage branching; French and Signet types need no pinching.
records.source_context: Keep the seed and media moist by using a plastic cover over the seeding tray. Use a misting bottle to water. Seeds will germinate in 5 to 8 days at 70 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit. After germination, grow plants at 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit during the day and 65 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit at night.

records.our_prose: Soil warmth, not the calendar, is the real germination trigger: direct-sow into soil near 65 to 70 °F after frost and seedlings break ground in 5 to 8 days. Go light on nitrogen and avoid overwatering, both of which give leaves at the expense of bloom; deadhead or cut for the vase to sustain flowering to frost. For root-knot nematode pressure, grow French types (Tagetes patula) as a dense, solid cover stand for two months before the susceptible crop, then turn them under, rather than scattering a few among the vegetables.

records.our_prose: Choose by type and purpose. French marigolds (Tagetes patula) are the compact, bushy, long-blooming bedding and edging workhorses and the type to use for root-knot nematode cover plantings (cultivars such as 'Single Gold' and 'Tangerine' are the trialed performers). African or American marigolds (Tagetes erecta) are the tall, large-pompon types for the back of the border and for cutting; they benefit most from deadheading and staking. Signet marigolds (Tagetes tenuifolia) are the petite, lacy, heat- and drought-tough edgers, smothered in small single flowers whose petals are edible. Single, open-faced flowers serve pollinators better than the densest doubles.

records.source_context: Watering Marigolds Water marigolds well at planting and keep the soil evenly moist for the first couple of weeks until they become established. After establishment, marigolds grow well with about one inch of water per week. In the absence of adequate rainfall, water the soil deeply once a week, allowing it to dry somewhat between waterings.
